key: I do not exculpate myself. Lo! the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil, save that whereon my Lord hath mercy.
s: Joseph is cleared when the ruler’s wife confesses before the king; Ibn Kathir, on 12:50 to 12:53, reads it as her words, confessing the desire behind her advances, since Joseph was not yet present, and al-Tabari, on 12:53, as Joseph’s own, admitting that souls urge what they desire unless his Lord has mercy.

evidence.words: تَقُولُ الْمَرْأَةُ: وَلَسْتُ أُبَرِّئُ نَفْسِي، فَإِنَّ النَّفْسَ تَتَحَدَّثُ وَتَتَمَنَّى؛ وَلِهَذَا رَاوَدَتْهُ لِأَنَّهَا أَمَارَةٌ بِالسُّوءِ … وَالْقَوْلُ الْأَوَّلُ أَقْوَى وَأُظْهِرُ؛ لِأَنَّ سِيَاقَ الْكَلَامِ كُلِّهِ مِنْ كَلَامِ امْرَأَةِ الْعَزِيزِ بِحَضْرَةِ الْمَلِكِ، وَلَمْ يَكُنْ يُوسُفُ، عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ، عِنْدَهُمْ، بَلْ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَحْضَرَهُ الْمَلِكُ … يقول يوسف صلوات الله عليه: وما أبرئ نفسي من الخطأ والزلل فأزكيها … إن النفوسَ نفوسَ العباد، تأمرهم بما تهواه، وإن كان هواها في غير ما فيه رضا الله … إلا أن يرحم ربي من شاء من خلقه
evidence.gloss: (Ibn Kathir, on 12:50 to 12:53:) The woman says: I do not absolve myself, for the soul talks and wishes, and that is why she solicited him, because it commands evil … The first saying is the stronger and more evident, because the whole course of the speech is the words of the ruler’s wife in the presence of the king, and Joseph was not with them; the king had him brought only after that … (al-Tabari, on 12:53:) Joseph, God’s blessings on him, says: I do not absolve myself of error and slips so as to call myself pure … the souls of God’s servants command them to what they desire, even when their desire lies outside what pleases God … except that my Lord has mercy on whom He will of His creatures.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Yusuf 12:53, at 1648; the first two sentences of the ayah, 19 words). Plain sense faithful to day.js: in 12:50 to 12:51 the king summons the women and the ruler’s wife confesses that she asked an evil act of Joseph and that he is truthful; the clause does not decide who speaks 12:53 (Pickthall’s parenthesis in 12:52 gives it to Joseph) and takes no four-word run from the key. Two commentators, a genuine and classic difference, named and not resolved. Ibn Kathir, in his one comment on 12:50 to 12:53, glosses the ayah as the woman’s words (the soul talks and wishes, which is why she solicited him), calls it the better known view, and closes that it is stronger because the whole speech is hers before the king and Joseph was not yet with them; he also notes that Ibn Jarir relates only the Joseph view. Al-Tabari on 12:53 opens by glossing the ayah as Joseph’s own words: he does not absolve himself of error, souls command what they desire, except whom his Lord has mercy on; the chains he then cites all make Joseph the speaker. Both readings are theirs as paraphrased. Evidence pieces re-found in the packet. Under 60 words for two commentators; entry-check ok. Marked sexual only because the reading names her advances, plainly and without detail.
